items.title: My Sign-Ins will let a user with a passkey, FIDO2 key or Windows Hello set a new password without knowing the old one; rollout moves up to mid-October and the switch is tenant-wide only
items.officialTitle: (Updated) Microsoft Entra: Authenticated password change in My Sign-Ins
items.fingerprint: Microsoft revised MC1437671 on 7 October 2026. The title changes from 'Passwordless password change in My Sign-Ins' to 'Authenticated password change in My Sign-Ins'; general availability, Worldwide and GCC, now begins in mid-October 2026 where it read late October, and still completes by late October; and the post now says 'The setting is tenant-wide: you can turn it on for your entire tenant or leave it off for everyone. There is no per-user or per-group scoping.' A user who has a passkey, FIDO2 security key or Windows Hello for Business can set a new password from My Sign-Ins without knowing the current one and without SSPR. Off by default; Microsoft says Learn documentation arrives with the release.
items.why: With the feature on, holding one phishing-resistant credential is enough to replace the account's password, so a passkey an attacker managed to register becomes a way to set a known password for anything that still accepts one. The control is all or nothing: privileged accounts cannot be left out.
items.action: Leave it off until the Learn page is published. If it is turned on, alert on a password change that follows a new passkey or FIDO2 registration on the same account within a short interval.

items.title: Sentinel gets an ASIM EmailEvent schema, and the ASIM parser list gains its first Agent Event parser
items.officialTitle: Introducing the Microsoft Sentinel ASIM EmailEvent schema
items.fingerprint: The Microsoft Sentinel blog of 7 October 2026 says the ASIM EmailEvent schema 'is now available', and the schema reference is on Learn: one normalised shape for email delivery and inspection records from mail servers, secure email gateways and email security services, with EventType and EventSubType, EmailFromAddress and EmailToRecipients, EmailSubject, EmailFiles and EmailUrls, SPF, DKIM and DMARC results, DvcAction and EmailDeliveryLocation. The ASIM parsers list, dated 7 October on Learn, gains an Agent Event parsers section with one source: Anthropic Claude Compliance events collected through the Codeless Connector Framework by BlueVoyant, parser _Im_AgentEvent_AnthropicClaudeCompliance. The parsers list names no EmailEvent source parser yet.
items.why: An email rule written against EmailEvents covers Defender for Office 365 only. A normalised schema lets one analytic rule read a third-party gateway and Defender together, with the email authentication results as named fields. No source parser is listed yet, so today the schema is a target to build to rather than something a rule can query.
items.action: No action required. If a secure email gateway feeds Sentinel, check whether its connector ships an EmailEvent parser before writing new email rules against the source tables.

items.title: Microsoft removes the rollout notes from system-preferred authentication and the registration campaign: both are now documented as every tenant’s behaviour

The system-preferred authentication page no longer says the Microsoft managed state 'affects both first-factor and multifactor authentication and is being gradually deployed to tenants through September 2026'; the commit is titled 'Remove completed system-preferred rollout note'. The registration campaign page no longer says 'We're rolling out this version of the registration campaign. The rollout is expected to finish by the end of September 2026.' Neither page gained text.

items.title: Defender for Office 365 starts detecting malicious URLs inside QR codes in Teams messages after delivery, and the detections reach Advanced Hunting
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Defender for Office 365: Post-delivery protection for malicious QR codes in Microsoft Teams
items.fingerprint: Defender for Office 365 extends Teams URL protection to URLs inside QR codes. Teams messages containing a QR code are analysed after delivery; a malicious URL puts a warning on the message in external and in internal conversations, and with Defender for Office 365 Plan 1 or Plan 2 and Teams ZAP enabled eligible malicious internal messages may be blocked. Microsoft says the detections appear in Advanced Hunting 'with QRCode in the UrlLocation column of the MessageUrlInfo table'. General availability, Worldwide, from early October to early November 2026; it is part of existing Teams URL protection and has no separate setting. The MessageUrlInfo schema page on Learn, read on 8 October, lists six columns and UrlLocation is not yet among them.
items.why: A QR code was the way round URL scanning in Teams chat, because the link sits inside an image. This is the first time a QR-borne URL in Teams becomes a record a hunt can read, and the column Microsoft names for it is not in the published schema yet, so a query that names it directly may fail until the rollout reaches the tenant.
items.action: No action required by Microsoft. Confirm Teams ZAP is on, and add the QR code hunt in Hunting to the Teams phishing playbook; it is written to run before and after the UrlLocation column arrives.

items.title: Defender Vulnerability Management starts covering Node.js, Python and Java packages on Windows; assessment exports grow and gain a ProductCategory field
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management: Private preview for selected developer package vulnerability coverage
items.fingerprint: Defender Vulnerability Management adds CVE coverage for a curated set of Node.js, Python and Java packages on Windows devices onboarded to Defender for Endpoint: Targeted Release late September to late October, public preview late October to late November and general availability late November to late December 2026, Worldwide. Findings appear in the existing software component, vulnerability, affected device and recommendation views. A ProductCategory value separates Applications, Components and BIOS/firmware records; complete-file assessment exports for enabled tenants carry the full package population, JSON exports can be filtered server-side, and ProductCategory 'may not be enabled' in the Advanced Hunting tables during the initial preview. Microsoft states it is not an SBOM and carries no dependency graph, reachability analysis or package ownership.
items.why: Every pipeline that pulls vulnerability assessment exports into a SIEM, a data lake or a ticketing tool sees more rows per device once this is on, and the new rows are components rather than installed applications. A dashboard that counts vulnerable software per device changes its number with no new exposure behind it.
items.action: Record current export file sizes and ingestion times now. When the tenant is enabled, filter downloads by ProductCategory or apply Microsoft's Legacy Components Support List, and set a new baseline for any Delta integration.

items.officialTitle: Microsoft Edge: Retiring legacy sign-in implementation on Windows
items.fingerprint: From Microsoft Edge version 157 on Windows the legacy direct-WAM sign-in implementation is retired and all remaining profiles move to the OneAuth authentication library; the 'fallback legacy WAM path will default off under all circumstances', which includes organisations that disabled OneAuth with --disable-features=msOneAuthWAM. Windows Web Account Manager itself is not deprecated; OneAuth continues to use it. General availability, Worldwide and GCC, begins and completes in early November 2026. Microsoft says most users move transparently and in rare cases must sign in to Edge again. edge://signin-internals shows OneAuth or WAM under Edge Auth Library Information, and msedge.exe --enable-features=msForceOneAuthWAM tests the move on version 155 or later. Marked a major change.
items.why: Microsoft names browser sign-in, token fetch, single sign-on and account synchronisation as the affected experiences. A profile that loses its sign-in after the update stops presenting the signed-in work account to web applications, which reaches the SOC as extra prompts and Conditional Access failures rather than as an Edge fault (inferred).
items.action: Check edge://signin-internals on a sample of managed profiles, remove any --disable-features=msOneAuthWAM switch from deployment, and pilot msForceOneAuthWAM on Edge 155 or later before version 157 arrives in early November.

items.officialTitle: Microsoft 365: Targeted Release retirement
items.fingerprint: Targeted release for Microsoft 365 retires in January 2027 and is replaced by three release options: Frontier (preview), Standard release (at general availability) and Deferred release (eligible major updates about 30 days after Standard release begins). In November 2026 administrators can no longer add, remove or modify Targeted release enrolments and a unified release preferences experience opens in the Microsoft 365 admin center; Message Center gives 31 October 2026 as the act-by date. Users already enrolled keep receiving Targeted release features until the retirement. Marked a major change; it names Teams, new Outlook, Outlook on the web, Office for the web, OneDrive, SharePoint Online and some components of Exchange Online.
items.why: Targeted release is how a pilot ring sees a change before the rest of the tenant, security-relevant changes included. From November the ring is frozen as it stands; from January the only early ring is Frontier, and Deferred release becomes the first option that holds a major update back by about 30 days.
items.action: Before 31 October export who is enrolled in Targeted release (Settings > Org settings > Organization profile > Release preferences), decide which of them move to Frontier, and decide whether the tenant default becomes Standard or Deferred release.

items.title: Conditional Access for agents: the prerequisite now names Agent 365 or Microsoft 365 E7, and a policy scoped through Users never reaches agent user accounts
items.officialTitle: Secure autonomous agents with Conditional Access
items.publishedNote: Microsoft prints no date for the change (inferred): entra-docs commits 965931b7ff and 6e8eb8aa25 of 7 October 2026, merged with pull request 14521 at 16:36 UTC, and read on the published Learn page the same evening.
items.fingerprint: Two Conditional Access pages for agent identities changed on 7 October 2026. Prerequisites of the autonomous-agents page read 'A Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 license.' and 'Agent 365 license will soon be required'; they now read 'One of the following license plans: Microsoft 365 E7, which includes Agent 365 and Microsoft Entra Suite, to protect access for both users and agents. Microsoft Agent 365, paired with: Microsoft Entra ID P1 or Microsoft 365 E3 for Conditional Access. Microsoft Entra ID P2 or Microsoft 365 E5 when using agent risk-based Conditional Access.' The companion page 'Conditional Access for agents' now states: 'Policies scoped through the "Users" assignment don't apply to agent user accounts. This boundary applies whether the policy targets all users, selected users, groups, directory roles, or external users.' and 'Selecting an agent identity as the policy subject doesn't cover agent requests made on behalf of the user.'
items.why: Two things a SOC assumes about Conditional Access stop being true for agents. A policy that targets agent identities is documented as needing Agent 365 or Microsoft 365 E7, where Entra ID P1 or P2 was listed alone; and an 'All users' policy does not cover an agent's user account however that account is selected. Microsoft does not state what happens to existing agent policies in a tenant without the licence.
items.action: List the Conditional Access policies that target agent identities or agent users, confirm the tenant holds Agent 365 or Microsoft 365 E7, and add a policy under Assignments, Agents, Agent Users wherever an all-users policy was assumed to cover agent user accounts.

items.title: Azure RBAC: Microsoft confirms customer-managed deny assignments exist in private preview, and warns that reference pages may already show the commands
items.officialTitle: List Azure deny assignments
items.publishedNote: The page's own date moved from 24 April 2025 to 6 October 2026 (azure-docs commit 3bd30651ed4c); it reached the main branch after the morning read and was read on the published Learn page on 7 October.
items.fingerprint: The Important note read 'You can't directly create your own deny assignments. Deny assignments are created and managed by Azure.' It now reads 'Customer-managed deny assignments are currently in private preview. The availability of related APIs or commands in generated reference documentation doesn't indicate that the feature is in public preview or generally available. For generally available scenarios, Azure creates and manages deny assignments.' The following section drops the sentence 'You can't directly create your own deny assignments.'
items.why: A deny assignment overrides every role assignment at its scope, Owner included. Microsoft now states that a tenant-authored form exists in private preview and that API or command reference may show it before release, so a deny assignment found in a subscription is no longer proof that Azure or a deployment stack wrote it. This moves an access control boundary, which is why it is weighted as identity and not as Azure platform.
items.action: No action stated by Microsoft. Baseline the deny assignments that exist today per subscription (Get-AzDenyAssignment) so a later customer-written one stands out, and decide who would be allowed to write them before the feature reaches public preview.

items.fingerprint: Roadmap entry 561320, created 5 May 2026; on 6 October 2026 its status changed from In development to Launched. Microsoft writes: 'In Word, Excel, and PowerPoint, the ‘Prevent some connected experiences that analyze content’ label setting now prevents files in these apps from being sent to all Microsoft connected experiences for analysis, rather than a subset of these connected experiences.'
items.why: A label that already carries this setting now withholds labelled files from every connected experience that analyses content. That is a wider data boundary without a policy change, and users of those labels may find features that worked yesterday unavailable on labelled files.
items.action: List the sensitivity labels that carry the setting, tell their owners that its reach has widened, and expect help-desk questions about missing connected features on files with those labels.

items.publishedNote: (inferred) Microsoft prints no day for this line: it sits under the August 2026 preview heading of the what's-new page, whose ms.date is 1 October 2026, and this brief first read it on 7 October 2026.
items.title: Custom detection rules can keep their alerts out of incident correlation: a new incidentConfiguration setting creates standalone, single-alert incidents (Graph beta)
items.officialTitle: Added the incidentConfiguration property to the detectionAction resource and the incidentConfiguration complex type
items.fingerprint: Microsoft Graph what's new, Security, beta: 'Added the incidentConfiguration property to the detectionAction resource and the incidentConfiguration complex type. Use this setting to exclude alerts generated by a custom detection rule from automatic incident correlation and create standalone, single-alert incidents.' The line was not on the page when this brief read it on 6 October and is there on 7 October.
items.why: Correlation is how Defender XDR folds a rule's alerts into a larger incident. A rule that opts out produces one incident per alert: useful for a detection that must never be merged into someone else's incident, and a way to flood or fragment the queue if set carelessly. It is also a rule property that can be changed through the API by anything holding CustomDetection.ReadWrite.All.
items.action: Decide which custom detections, if any, should create standalone incidents, set the property deliberately on those, and add the property to whatever reviews changes to detection rules so a silent switch does not split an attack across single-alert incidents.

They can be filtered, searched and exported to CSV, and 'Role-based access controls will apply. Administrators will only be able to view logs for workloads they are authorized to manage.' items.why: A restore is a bulk write over production data and a backup policy change decides what can be recovered after ransomware, and until now neither had a log inside the product. The post does not say whether these events also reach the unified audit log, so the admin center page and its CSV export are the only place Microsoft has promised them.
items.action: After mid-October open Microsoft 365 Backup, Recent activities, confirm that policy changes and restores are listed with the administrator who made them, and decide whether the CSV export needs to be collected on a schedule until the same events are confirmed in the unified audit log.

items.deadlineNote: Microsoft states the Worldwide rollout runs from early November to mid-November 2026 and prints no calendar day, so no deadline date is carried.
items.title: Purview DLP for unmanaged apps in Edge for Business will work in tenants that use Intune multi-admin approval, and Purview can hand the Intune step to an Intune administrator as a task
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Purview DLP: Improved setup and Intune multi-admin approval support for unmanaged apps in Edge for Business
items.fingerprint: Message Center post of 6 October 2026, tag Admin impact. Microsoft Purview will 'support tenants that use Intune multi-admin approval' when data loss prevention for unmanaged apps in Edge for Business is set up, and the portal will show 'clearer setup status information, more detailed error information, and guidance'. A Purview administrator can 'send a task to the appropriate Intune administrator'; Microsoft adds that this 'does not grant permissions, bypass approval requirements, or automatically complete requested Intune changes.' Worldwide rollout early November to mid-November 2026; 'No action is required before rollout.'
items.why: Multi-admin approval is the control that stops one Intune administrator changing policy alone, and until now it stood in the way of this DLP setup. Microsoft says the hand-off does not bypass approval, which is the sentence to hold it to: after rollout, an approval request raised from Purview is a new way for an Intune change to be asked for.
items.action: If Intune multi-admin approval is on, tell the approvers that requests originating from the Purview portal will begin to appear in November, and check after rollout that the setup status in Purview matches what Intune actually applied.

items.title: Defender for Identity sensor v3.x can now be activated on a domain controller without Defender for Endpoint as a generally available path, for new deployments only

It is also a new onboarding package that touches tier-0 hosts, and it does not migrate v2.x sensors.

items.title: Attack disruption identity exclusions: with Unified RBAC on, Core security settings (manage) is now required for both the Defender for Endpoint and the Defender for Identity data source
items.officialTitle: Exclude assets from automated responses in automatic attack disruption
items.publishedNote: ms.date on the page moved from 7 August 2026 to 4 October 2026; the edit reached the published page between 13:25 and 17:48 UTC on 4 October (merill/defender-docs-mirror 86e9a93 to b30ef89).
items.tier0Note: Who may exempt an account from automatic disabling during an attack. It governs a response control, not a write path into AD DS, a sync agent, a CA or a Global-Administrator-equivalent role.
items.fingerprint: Microsoft rewrote the permissions for identity exclusions in automatic attack disruption, page dated 4 October 2026. New text: "Identity exclusions affect automated response actions in both Defender for Identity and Defender for Endpoint." With Unified RBAC enabled the requirement is now a Security Operator (or higher) global Microsoft Entra role, or the Core security settings (manage) permission "for the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint and Microsoft Defender for Identity data sources. If either product isn't deployed, permission for its data source isn't required." The row for Unified RBAC disabled now reads "Disabled for identities and endpoints"; the device-exclusion table is unchanged.
items.why: An identity exclusion stops attack disruption from disabling that account, so the right to add one is the right to switch a containment control off for a chosen identity. Microsoft now states that right is scoped per data source: a custom Unified RBAC role holding Core security settings (manage) for only one of the two products is, by this text, not enough where both are deployed.
items.action: No deadline is stated. List the custom Unified RBAC roles that hold Core security settings (manage), note which data sources each covers, and review who can edit Settings > Microsoft Defender XDR > Automated response > Identities; alert on changes to that exclusion list.

Existing configurations aren't affected and continue to be supported. If your organization requires these capabilities, contact Microsoft Support." The role descriptions themselves are unchanged and the Add additional admins procedure on the same page still mentions selecting App/Instance admin.

With new assignments closed, the next person who needs that scope gets a broader role instead, or a support case; existing scoped admins are untouched.

items.title: Application Gateway WAF: geo-based custom rules reach IPv6 traffic only after a preview feature is registered, and only on a dual-stack gateway
items.officialTitle: IPv6 geo-based custom rules for Azure Web Application Firewall (preview)
items.tier0Note: A network protection control in front of web applications; it opens no write path into AD DS, a sync agent, a CA or a privileged role.
items.fingerprint: Microsoft published a new article on 3 October 2026 (azure-docs commit 19d165730d, merged 05:08 UTC; the page's own ms.date is 17 September 2026). Geomatch custom rules in Application Gateway WAF v2 are extended to IPv6 traffic as a preview, and only for a subscription that registers the feature AllowAppGwWafIpv6Geo in Microsoft.Network. The gateway must be dual-stack on both its public and private IP configuration; an IPv4-only gateway cannot be converted and IPv6-only gateways are not supported. Registration is not needed for managed rule sets, for non-geo IPv6 custom rules or for logging. The platform refuses to associate a policy holding IPv6 geo rules with a dual-stack gateway that cannot evaluate them.
items.why: A geo-block is a control SOC teams count on. Microsoft now documents that evaluating IPv6 traffic against geomatch custom rules on Application Gateway WAF needs an opt-in preview feature and a dual-stack gateway, so a country block written for IPv4 should not be assumed to cover IPv6 clients (inferred from the registration requirement; Microsoft does not describe the behaviour without it).
items.action: List Application Gateway WAF policies with geomatch custom rules, check whether their gateways have an IPv6 frontend, and test a blocked country over IPv6 before relying on the rule; register AllowAppGwWafIpv6Geo only after accepting preview terms.

items.title: Copilot DLP policies become manageable per administrative unit: scoped admins create, edit and delete them inside their unit from late October
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Purview | Data Loss Prevention: Administrative Units support for DLP policies for Microsoft Copilot

items.title: Provisioning expressions gain NormalizeDiacriticsByCulture: German umlauts become ae, oe, ue and ss when the culture is "de"
items.officialTitle: Reference for writing expressions for attribute mappings in Microsoft Entra Application Provisioning
items.tier0Note: A string function for attribute mappings; it changes what a mapping can produce, not who can write to AD DS, a sync agent or a privileged role.
items.fingerprint: Microsoft added one function to the provisioning expression reference on 3 October 2026 (entra-docs commit 231747abc5, merged 07:35 UTC; ms.date 2 October 2026). NormalizeDiacriticsByCulture(source, culture) takes two required strings; with culture "de" it transliterates ä, ö, ü and ß to ae, oe, ue and ss (Müller becomes Mueller). "de" is the only supported culture value, and any other value behaves exactly as NormalizeDiacritics. Nothing else on the page changed.
items.why: Low for a SOC. It matters only where an identity team switches an existing mapping to the new function: generated user names, mail nicknames or UPN prefixes for German names then change form, and watchlists or detections keyed on the old spelling stop matching.
items.action: No action stated by Microsoft. If the identity team adopts the function in a UPN or mailNickname mapping, ask for the change date so identity-keyed detections can be checked.

items.title: Microsoft withdrew the External ID credential management API reference four days after publishing it: customer passkey self-service goes back to the Graph FIDO2 provisioning APIs
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Entra External ID credential management API reference
items.tier0Note: Applies to external (customer) tenants and acts only on the signed-in customer's own credentials; it opens no write path into AD DS, a sync agent, a CA or a privileged role.
items.fingerprint: entra-docs commit 9608dc10c3 of 6 October 2026, 'Revert passkey credential management documentation (#14532)', deletes the 587-line credential management API reference published on 2 October and redirects its address to the Microsoft Graph fido2AuthenticationMethod resource. The external-tenant passkey how-to, re-dated 6 October, now reads 'Use the FIDO2 provisioning APIs to build this into your app' where it read 'Use the credential management API to build this experience with low-privilege delegated permissions', and answers 'No' where it answered 'Yes' to whether signed-in customers can register their own passkeys with delegated permissions. The sample is described as 'administrator-controlled provisioning with high-privilege application permissions ... intended for testing only'. The same reference was removed once before, on 9 September. Whether the resource application 6bf38b3c-a70f-49aa-a1d9-10e4cc74dde9 and its Me.UserAuthenticationMethod.* permissions still exist in the service is not stated by Microsoft.
items.why: The low-privilege route for a customer to register a passkey is undocumented again, so an external-tenant application that wants passkey registration is pointed back at Graph application permissions over authentication methods, which is the high-privilege pattern the withdrawn page replaced. An app built against the withdrawn API between 2 and 6 October now depends on something Microsoft no longer describes.
items.action: In external tenants, keep the alert on a service principal for appId 6bf38b3c-a70f-49aa-a1d9-10e4cc74dde9, find any app that was granted Me.UserAuthenticationMethod.* since 2 October and ask its owner what it now calls, and review every app holding UserAuthenticationMethod.ReadWrite.All for passkey provisioning. Workforce tenants need no action.
items.fingerprintBefore: Microsoft published a new reference page on 2 October 2026 (entra-docs commit 75ba36fed9). The credential management API, at https://{tenant-subdomain}.ciamlogin.com/{tenant-id}/api/v1.0/me/..., lets a signed-in customer list and register passkeys; deletion is 'coming soon' and still goes through Microsoft Graph. It is a separate Microsoft-published resource, appId 6bf38b3c-a70f-49aa-a1d9-10e4cc74dde9, whose service principal must be created by hand until automatic provisioning is available. Accepted delegated permissions: Me.UserAuthenticationMethod.Passkey.Read, Me.UserAuthenticationMethod.Read, Me.UserAuthenticationMethod.Passkey.ReadWrite and Me.UserAuthenticationMethod.ReadWrite. The external-tenant passkey how-to now points here instead of the Graph FIDO2 provisioning APIs.

items.title: App instance property lock: Microsoft now documents it for single-tenant apps too, and as on by default for new apps since June 2026
items.officialTitle: How to configure app instance property lock for your applications
items.publishedNote: ms.date 10/01/2026 as Microsoft prints it; the commit 955f195b95 landed on 2 October 2026 at 13:15 UTC, after the morning pass.

items.fingerprint: Microsoft rewrote the scope sentence from 'sensitive properties of a multitenant application object to be locked for modification after the application is provisioned in another tenant' to 'sensitive properties of an application's service principal to be locked for modification. It applies to both single-tenant and multitenant applications.' items.action: Query applications where servicePrincipalLockConfiguration is absent or isEnabled is false — single-tenant apps included — and enable the lock with all sensitive properties; apps created before June 2026 are the likely gap.

items.officialTitleNote: Microsoft publishes no announcement for this; the change is visible only as a diff of the Microsoft Graph service principal.
items.title: ThreatHunting.ReadWrite.All became grantable in the Graph service principal: run hunts and write hunting functions
items.reference: no MC/RM post — service principal only

items.title: AD FS DKM container ACL hardening enforcement (CVE-2026-56155)
items.fingerprint: Enforcement mode for AD FS DKM container ACL hardening (CVE-2026-56155) begins with the October 2026 Windows security update; supported Windows Server versions remediate by default unless admins opt out, and Event ID 1132 in the AD FS Admin log flags containers that need attention.
items.officialTitle: 60-Day Reminder: AD FS DKM container ACL hardening begins in October 2026
items.tier0Note: AD FS DKM container ACL hardening changes the permissions on the key material that signs federation tokens — a direct tier-0 federation asset.
items.deadlineNote: (inferred) Microsoft's 30-day reminder MC1471963 (14 Sep 2026) says enforcement begins with the October 2026 Windows security update; the second Tuesday of October 2026 is 13 October. Windows Server 2012 and 2012 R2 are not auto-remediated.
items.why: The ACLs being hardened are on the key material that signs federation tokens. Enforcement arrives with the October Windows security update and is on by default, so this changes an AD FS server whether or not anyone plans for it — and Windows Server 2012 and 2012 R2 are not remediated automatically at all.
items.action: Before the October update, check the AD FS Admin log for Event ID 1132 on every federation server and clear what it flags. On Windows Server 2012 and 2012 R2 the remediation is manual and nothing will do it for you.

items.tier0Note: Automatic remediation of the AD FS token-signing key container — the Golden SAML target — on every supported server that does not opt out.
items.deadlineNote: Microsoft states enforcement begins with the October 2026 Windows security update; 13 October 2026 is that update's release date.
items.why: The DKM container holds the key material behind AD FS token signing. A loose ACL there is the Golden SAML precondition. Microsoft is about to fix it for you, which is good — and to change permissions on a domain object under your federation service without asking, which needs a maintenance window.
items.action: Install the July 2026 or later Windows update on every AD FS server, then read the AD FS Admin log for Event ID 1132 and fix what it names before 13 October. Windows Server 2012 and 2012 R2 get no automatic remediation — do those by hand.
items.title: AD FS DKM container ACL hardening switches from audit to enforcement with the October Windows update
items.officialTitle: 30-Day Reminder: AD FS DKM container ACL hardening begins in October 2026
items.fingerprint: From the October 2026 Windows security update, supported Windows Server versions will run remediation of insecure AD FS Distributed Key Manager container ACLs by default unless an administrator opts out, addressing the elevation-of-privilege vulnerability CVE-2026-56155. Windows Server 2012 and 2012 R2 are not remediated automatically and still need manual work.

items.fingerprint: Access to some resources now goes through stricter Conditional Access evaluation, which can break sign-in on Teams Rooms on Android, Teams phones, displays and panels from app version 1449/1.0.96.2026249711. items.title: App Governance permissions change for three Entra roles as Defender XDR Unified RBAC takes over
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps: Permission changes for select App Governance Entra roles
items.deadlineNote: Microsoft writes: “We will begin rolling out in mid-October 2026 and expect to complete by late October 2026.”
items.tier0Note: Touches a tier-0 control: Conditional Access, an authentication method, a privileged role or an app consent path.
items.fingerprint: App Governance in Defender for Cloud Apps moves to Defender XDR Unified RBAC. Cloud App Security Administrator GAINS permission to view and manage App Governance policies; Compliance Administrator LOSES the ability to manage App Governance policies and to enable or disable App Governance in Settings; Compliance Data Administrator LOSES the ability to enable or disable App Governance in Settings; custom Defender XDR Unified RBAC roles for Defender for Cloud Apps gain App Governance access. items.title: Microsoft corrected PIM for Groups: eligible members and owners are credential-protected too, and changing those credentials needs Privileged Authentication Administrator
items.officialTitle: What is Privileged Identity Management for groups?
items.tier0Note: The article governs who may reset the credentials of members and owners of a role-assignable group, which is the write path used to elevate into Entra roles including Global Administrator.
items.fingerprint: Pull request 2049 reached entra-docs main at 16:57 UTC on 23 September 2026 and the live branch at 17:42 UTC. It widened the stated protection of role-assignable groups from active members to members and owners including eligible ones who have not activated, and it replaced the Helpdesk Administrator example in the security note with a general statement plus a new sentence naming Privileged Authentication Administrator as the least role that can change those credentials. The include file's ms.date moved from 01/31/2023 to 07/29/2026.
items.why: The previous wording left open the classic PIM-for-Groups attack: a lower-privileged admin resets the password of a user who is only an eligible member of a role-assignable group, then activates the assignment on their behalf. Microsoft now states that the credential protection already covers eligible members and owners, so that path is closed by the platform — but only for groups that were actually created as role-assignable.
items.action: Confirm that every group used to elevate into an Entra role is role-assignable (isAssignableToRole true). A group that is not gets none of this protection, and the eligible-member reset path is still open on it. No deadline is stated by Microsoft.

items.title: Microsoft corrects what PIM for Groups actually protects: eligible members and owners were always in scope, and non-role-assignable groups never were
items.officialTitle: Privileged Identity Management for Groups
items.publishedNote: The page still prints ms.date 23 April 2026; the correction reached the public entra-docs live branch on 22 September 2026 and Microsoft did not bump the printed date.
items.tier0Note: The corrected sentence describes who can reset the credentials of a user who can elevate to an Entra role.
items.fingerprint: Microsoft replaced the statement that for role-assignable groups no other users can change the credentials of the users who are active members, with: credential protection covers the members and owners of the group, including eligible members and owners who have not activated yet. The accompanying note adds that groups used for role elevation must be created as role-assignable, and that changing the credentials of members and owners of a role-assignable group requires at least the Privileged Authentication Administrator role.
items.why: The old sentence understated the protection in one direction and overstated it in another. The practical consequence is the second half: a group that grants an Entra role but was not created role-assignable gives its eligible members no credential protection at all, so a Helpdesk, Authentication or User Administrator can reset their password and then elevate. That is a documented escalation path, and it is a configuration mistake rather than a vulnerability.
items.action: List every group that grants an Entra role and check isAssignableToRole on each. Any that is false is the finding; it cannot be changed after creation, so the group has to be recreated as role-assignable and the assignments moved.

items.title: Eight Graph permissions became grantable in the service principal: app certificate trust configuration, cross-tenant content migration and workbooks
items.officialTitleNote: Microsoft publishes no announcement for this; the change is visible only as a diff of the Microsoft Graph service principal.
items.reference: no MC/RM post — service principal only
items.tier0Note: AppCertTrustConfiguration.ReadWrite.All writes the tenant's application certificate trust configuration, which governs which certificates an application may authenticate with.
items.fingerprint: Between the 17 September and the 22 September dumps of the Microsoft Graph service principal, application roles went from 741 to 747 and delegated scopes from 825 to 827, with nothing removed. The six new application roles are AppCertTrustConfiguration.Read.All, AppCertTrustConfiguration.ReadWrite.All, CrossTenantContentMigration.Read.All, CrossTenantContentMigration.ReadWrite.All, Workbooks.Read.All and Workbooks.ReadWrite.All; the two new delegated scopes are Workbooks.Read.All and Workbooks.ReadWrite.All. All eight are enabled. AppCertTrustConfiguration had existed as a delegated scope since 9 May 2026 but reaches application scope only now.
items.why: Two of the eight are a consent surface worth naming. AppCertTrustConfiguration.ReadWrite.All is application-scoped write access to the tenant's app certificate trust configuration — the setting that decides which certificates an application may present to authenticate — so an app holding it can widen what counts as a trusted credential. CrossTenantContentMigration.ReadWrite.All is an application-scoped write over content moving between tenants, which is a bulk data path rather than a single-object one.
items.action: Nothing is granted by this change. Add all six application roles to the consent-review list now, before the first grant request arrives, and decide in advance which of them may ever be consented and by whom. Workbooks.* is the least alarming of the three families; the two AppCertTrustConfiguration roles are the ones to treat as privileged.

items.officialTitleNote: Microsoft publishes no title for this: the names are read out of the Graph service principal, which Microsoft does not document until later. The heading shown is the dump commit this brief read.

items.why: Two of them stand out. GroupMember.ReadBasic.All reads every group membership in the organisation as an application, with no signed-in user — that is the whole org chart and the membership of every privileged access group, in one call. And InfoProtectABACPolicy.ReadWrite.All plus InfoProtectAttributeAssignment.ReadWrite.All together let a holder define an attribute, assign it to a principal and thereby grant access to protected content without touching a group, a role or a label.
items.action: Put all ten appRoleIds on the consent-alert list today, ahead of the documentation. The two that matter most are 8222c640-cae5-4860-8d11-b32cfad95e03 (GroupMember.ReadBasic.All) and 4bfc1735-3a0c-4602-a159-9cfa07213339 (InfoProtectABACPolicy.ReadWrite.All). Then ask Purview whether an ABAC policy catalog is being enabled in this tenant, because nothing else has announced it.

items.reference: no MC/RM post — Microsoft Security Blog only
items.tier0Note: A service principal has no MFA, no sign-in risk and no user to call; it is the identity a Conditional Access policy does not see.
items.fingerprint: Microsoft Threat Intelligence published the Storm-3168 write-up on 25 September 2026, naming an actor that uses agentic tooling against compromised service principals for cloud reconnaissance and credential access.
items.why: Service principal abuse is the identity path with the least coverage in most Conditional Access designs, and this names the tradecraft.
items.action: Hunt for the described service-principal tradecraft, then review workload identity Conditional Access and credential lifetimes.

items.tier0Note: Interactive domain sign-in fails on affected Windows 11 devices because the machine secure channel with on-premises Active Directory breaks.
items.title: September update makes Windows 11 honour Machine Identity Isolation; devices not on a Windows Server 2025 domain functional level lose domain trust
items.officialTitle: Domain-joined devices might lose their secure trust relationship with the domain
items.reference: no MC/RM post — Windows release health
items.fingerprint: Opened 16 September 2026 (status Mitigated): after KB5124008 (24H2/25H2) or KB5124012 (26H1) and later updates, Windows begins honouring existing or policy-provisioned Machine Identity Isolation enforcement. The feature is supported only with domain controllers at Windows Server 2025 domain functional level; elsewhere Credential Guard protected machine accounts can lose their secure channel and users cannot sign in with valid domain credentials. Cached sign-in may still work; AD replication is not affected. Workaround: set MachineIdentityIsolation to 0 by the method that enabled it, restart, then run Test-ComputerSecureChannel -Repair. Microsoft plans to temporarily block enforcement in a future update.
items.why: A help-desk wave of 'trust relationship failed' sign-in errors after Patch Tuesday is this known issue, not an attack — but only if Machine Identity Isolation was enabled somewhere.
items.action: Find every Intune or Group Policy setting that enables Machine Identity Isolation; unless all DCs run Windows Server 2025 DFL, set it to 0 and repair the secure channel.

items.title: The 14 September out-of-band update fixes RDP instability and introduces an AD trust break on Credential Guard machines
items.officialTitle: September 14, 2026-KB5129195 (OS Builds 26200.9457 and 26100.9457) Out-of-band
items.tier0Note: A broken machine account trust takes Kerberos, Group Policy and device-based Conditional Access down with it.
items.fingerprint: Out-of-band cumulative updates KB5129195 (Windows 11 24H2 and 25H2) and KB5129194 (Windows 11 26H1) released 14 September 2026. They repair Remote Desktop Services instability and sign-in failures caused by the 8 September updates KB5124008 and KB5124012, and carry protections for CVE-2026-62721. Microsoft documents a new known issue: domain-joined machines protected by Credential Guard can lose the Active Directory trust relationship because of Machine Identity Isolation enforcement, with a registry, Intune and Group Policy workaround.
items.why: This is the rare update that fixes an outage and causes one: the trust-relationship failure removes a device from the domain entirely.
items.action: Deploy the out-of-band update where RDS is affected, and apply Microsoft's documented workaround on Credential Guard fleets before it lands.

items.title: SSPR registration campaign starts 5 October: users without enough registered methods are prompted, and directory-sourced phone and email stop working for reset on 7 November
items.fingerprint: Microsoft's post, last updated 4 August 2026, gives two dates. On 5 October 2026 the SSPR registration campaign begins prompting users and administrators to register authentication methods where the SSPR setting requires registration and they do not have enough. On 7 November 2026 enforcement begins: SSPR no longer accepts directory-sourced contact information (mobilePhone, businessPhone, otherMails) unless it was explicitly registered as an authentication method. Worldwide, GCC, GCC High and DoD; rollout early to mid-November. Microsoft says about 86% of SSPR verifications already use registered methods.
items.officialTitle: (Updated) Microsoft Entra ID SSPR will require registered authentication methods starting November 9, 2026
items.fingerprintBefore: Self-service password reset will require a registered authentication method from 5 October 2026, so users with none lose the reset path.
items.why: Nothing breaks on 5 October: that is the day the prompts start, so the help desk sees the change first. The break is on 7 November, when a user or administrator whose only reset path is a phone number or alternate email held in the directory can no longer reset a password. Until then a pre-populated directory attribute is an account-recovery path that the user never validated, which is the weakness Microsoft is closing.
items.action: In the Entra admin center open Authentication methods, User registration details, and list users and administrators with no registered method that satisfies the SSPR policy; leave the registration campaign enabled, warn the help desk that prompts begin on 5 October, and plan assisted registration for accounts that cannot self-register before 7 November.
items.deadlineNote: 5 October 2026 is the start of the registration campaign, not the enforcement date; enforcement is tracked as its own row, MC1325414-enforcement, on 7 November 2026. Microsoft prints three different November dates in the one post: 9 November in the title and the action line, 7 November for enforcement in the rollout schedule, and 6 November as the action-required date in the Message Center feed.

items.title: SMS first-factor sign-in retires for workforce tenants on 1 February 2027, worldwide and in GCC
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Entra ID: Follow-up on SMS first-factor sign-in retirement and upcoming changes
items.fingerprint: From 1 February 2027 users can no longer authenticate with a phone number and an SMS one-time passcode as a primary factor; existing SMS first-factor configurations stop being honoured, the management surface is removed from the Entra administration experiences, and sign-in attempts using a registered phone number with an SMS code are blocked. Users holding another registered method keep signing in. The retirement covers workforce tenants only and does not touch Azure AD B2C or External ID. It applies even where Choose Your Own Telephony Provider is used to keep SMS or voice as a multifactor method.
items.why: This is the first factor, not the second: a tenant that still allows SMS sign-in loses a working sign-in path on the date, not a convenience. Microsoft names passkeys, QR code authentication and FIDO2 keys as the alternatives, all of which need registration campaigns that take longer than the notice period suggests.
items.action: Run an authentication methods report for users with SMS sign-in enabled (SignInNoPassword), get them registered on a phishing-resistant method, and strip SMS first-factor dependencies out of the authentication method policy before 1 February 2027.

items.title: [Outlook Mobile] Purview DLP Wait-on-Send Support
items.officialTitle: (Updated) [Outlook Mobile] Purview DLP Wait-on-Send Support
items.fingerprint: Outlook for iOS and Android will support Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention wait-on-send policies, letting organizations require a DLP evaluation before an email is sent and configure how long users must wait for that evaluation to complete. This means sensitive information is inspected against organizational policy before messages leave the organization, with admins controlling the maximum wait time. General Availability rollout for Worldwide, GCC, GCC High and DoD begins and completes in late September 2026. Revised by Microsoft on 6 October 2026: general availability moved from late September to mid-November 2026.
items.why: Directly relevant to data protection: it closes the gap where mobile mail could leave the tenant before DLP evaluation finished, so DLP policy coverage and enforcement outcomes on mobile change.
items.action: Review existing Microsoft Purview DLP policies and, if wait-on-send enforcement is appropriate, enable and configure the desired wait period in supported DLP policies; no changes are required for organizations that will not use it.
items.revisedNote: Revised at source on 6 October 2026, found in the afternoon pass at 21:33 Warsaw.

items.title: Conditional Access now applies to Outlook attachment download, preview and upload
items.officialTitle: (Updated) Enhanced security and access controls for Outlook attachments
items.fingerprint: Outlook attachments run under a separate internal application configuration that inherits the Conditional Access policies assigned to the Exchange and Office cloud apps; users who fail a policy cannot download, preview or upload classic attachments, including inline images. Available now. Continuous Access Evaluation is not yet supported for this configuration. Microsoft revised the post at 16:32 UTC on 23 September 2026 and reversed its own statement about scoping: attachment-only Conditional Access policies are supported after all, through a first-party application named OwaDownloadAttachments, appId e4f2bb2d-a4d0-4eab-aac6-a8b83471cf64, for which a service principal must first be created in the tenant. Revised 29 September 2026: Microsoft now states the change applies only to Outlook on the web (OWA) and new Outlook.
items.why: Two things changed for a SOC. An exclusion you already made for Exchange Online does not carry over to attachments, so a user who can reach mail can still be blocked from downloading, previewing or uploading an attachment, and that will arrive as a help-desk ticket rather than as a policy change. And a new first-party application id now appears as a Conditional Access target resource, which is a name your policy review has never seen.
items.action: Re-read every Conditional Access policy that excludes Exchange Online and decide whether attachments should be excluded too. To scope attachments separately, create the service principal for appId e4f2bb2d-a4d0-4eab-aac6-a8b83471cf64 once (Cloud Application Administrator or Global Administrator, consent to Application.ReadWrite.All), then exclude or target OwaDownloadAttachments per policy.
items.fingerprintBefore: Outlook attachments run under a separate internal application configuration that inherits the Conditional Access policies assigned to the Exchange and Office cloud apps; users who fail a policy cannot download, preview or upload classic attachments, including inline images. items.revisionNote: Revised at source on 29 September at 20:13 UTC: the update banner moved from 23 to 29 September and one sentence was added, "Scope: This change is only applicable to Outlook web (OWA) and New Outlook." Nothing else in the body moved.

items.title: Two hidden Mail-Advanced permissions now name Office 365 Exchange Online as their resource application
items.officialTitleNote: Microsoft publishes no announcement for this; the change is visible only as a diff of permissions/new/provisioningInfo.json in the devx content repository.
items.reference: no MC/RM post — deployment map only
items.fingerprint: In the same 23 September sync, Mail-Advanced.ReadWrite (DelegatedWork, id f3af82f6-18e0-4a41-8dc8-a03c11854a8d) and Mail-Advanced.ReadWrite.All (Application, id e118f1da-5c1c-46cf-bff6-8858d786f46f) had their resourceAppId filled in for the first time: it moved from an empty string to 00000002-0000-0ff1-ce00-000000000000, which is Office 365 Exchange Online. Both are isHidden true and isEnabled true, and both are in this brief's inventory as documented Graph permissions.
items.why: The resource application decides which service principal the grant is recorded against. Naming Exchange Online rather than Microsoft Graph means a consent audit that reads only the Graph service principal will not see these two grants, and both are hidden and enabled, which is the combination that does not raise a consent prompt anyone reads.
items.action: When auditing mail-read consent, query the Office 365 Exchange Online service principal (00000002-0000-0ff1-ce00-000000000000) as well as the Graph one, and look for the two appRole ids above.

items.title: The deployment map gains UserCertificateIds.ReadWrite.All on the legacy Azure AD Graph resource and moves seven ResourcePolicy scopes off Microsoft Graph
items.officialTitle: Weekly Permissions sync 2026-09-24
items.fingerprint: provisioningInfo.json went from 1,942 to 1,943 names in the same 17:00 UTC commit. One name is new and seven changed resource. Microsoft publishes no date of its own for either, so the date beside them is the date the deployment map was read.
items.why: UserCertificateIds.ReadWrite.All is hidden, enabled and public in both Delegated and Application form, and it sits on the legacy Azure AD Graph resource rather than Microsoft Graph. A write path over the certificate identifiers bound to a user is a write path into how that user authenticates.
items.action: Nothing is grantable from this alone: the name is hidden and not in this tenant's service principal. Watch for it appearing in the tenant, and note that the seven ResourcePolicy scopes are no longer Microsoft Graph permissions.

Generally available worldwide now. Existing customer-owned app registrations keep working and need no change. items.title: Cloud Sync provisioning agent 1.1.2505.0 drops the Domain Admin requirement with a gMSA and removes Repair-AADCloudSyncToolsAccount
items.officialTitle: Microsoft Entra provisioning Agent: Version release history
items.tier0Note: The provisioning agent's service account is a hybrid identity write path into on-premises Active Directory.
items.fingerprint: Release date 21 September 2026, corrected from 16 September on 17 September. The release carries a security hardening section, and the agent no longer requires Domain Admin credentials when a gMSA with custom gMSA permissions is supplied. Repair-AADCloudSyncToolsAccount has been removed from the AADCloudSyncTools PowerShell module. Fixes cover unresolved cross-domain directory references causing object-level quarantine in AD2AADProvisioning jobs and domain controller affinity paging with nested OUs.
items.why: Dropping the Domain Admin requirement is a real reduction in standing privilege on the hybrid sync path, and it is available the moment the agent is upgraded. The removed cmdlet is the other half: any runbook that calls Repair-AADCloudSyncToolsAccount breaks on upgrade rather than warning.
items.action: Grep the automation estate for Repair-AADCloudSyncToolsAccount before upgrading. Then upgrade, and take the chance to move the agent onto a gMSA with custom permissions so the Domain Admin grant can be withdrawn.

items.title: Microsoft's DCU disrupts EvilTokens, a phishing-as-a-service platform built around device code flow and token theft
items.officialTitle: Unmasking EvilTokens: Getting to the root of device code phishing
items.fingerprint: Published 22 September 2026 on the Microsoft Security Blog. EvilTokens became one of the top phishing-as-a-service platforms by industrialising device code phishing with AI-assisted lures, automated infrastructure and token theft; Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit, with partners, facilitated a disruption of its infrastructure and operations.
items.why: Device code flow is still enabled by default in many tenants and produces a refresh token with no phishing-resistant factor anywhere in the path. A disruption removes one operator, not the technique.
items.action: Block device code flow in Conditional Access except for the named device classes that genuinely need it, and hunt sign-ins with authenticationProtocol deviceCode in the last 30 days.
items.tier0Note: Device code flow issues a refresh token for the signed-in account with no phishing-resistant factor anywhere in the path, so a successful lure against a privileged account is a Tier 0 credential.

items.title: NetworkAccess.Read.All and NetworkAccess.ReadWrite.All silently reach a new Global Secure Access secure-enterprise-browser endpoint
items.officialTitleNote: Microsoft publishes the reach change only in its own permissions data file; there is no release note.
items.reference: no MC/RM post — permissions data file only
items.tier0Note: NetworkAccess.ReadWrite.All now writes the Global Secure Access secure enterprise browser configuration, which is an enforcement control.
items.fingerprint: In the Weekly Permissions sync of 22 September 2026 (commit c1d06c5) NetworkAccess.Read.All gained GET /networkAccess/secureEnterpriseBrowserConfig and NetworkAccess.ReadWrite.All gained both GET and PATCH on the same path. No permission name was added or removed in that file, which stayed at 927 names, and no other scheme or privilege level moved.
items.why: This is the case with no consent prompt. Any application already holding NetworkAccess.ReadWrite.All — granted for network configuration reading — can now PATCH the secure enterprise browser configuration without anyone re-consenting or being asked. The reach of an existing grant widened; the grant did not.
items.action: List the applications holding NetworkAccess.ReadWrite.All in this tenant and confirm each one is still one you would grant that permission to today, knowing it now writes secure enterprise browser configuration. Add PATCH /networkAccess/secureEnterpriseBrowserConfig to what you watch in Graph activity logs.

items.title: Six Secure Score recommendations are grouped as an AI-Readiness device baseline, four of them new
items.officialTitle: New Microsoft Secure Score recommendations for AI-Readiness
items.fingerprint: Microsoft groups six device recommendations under an AI-Readiness tag in Exposure Management > Recommendations > Devices > Misconfigurations. Four are new: establish a hardware root of trust with TPM 2.0; isolate critical security functions with VBS; enforce kernel code integrity with HVCI; limit lateral movement with Windows LAPS. Two already existed: reduce unnecessary internet exposure on internet-facing devices, and protect the startup process with Secure Boot. The view shows affected devices, exposed critical devices, points achieved and the impact on the Devices Secure Score.
items.why: This is a named, filterable hardening baseline rather than six unrelated recommendations, and Windows LAPS plus HVCI are the two that most directly cut the paths an intruder uses after a first foothold. The AI-Readiness framing is Microsoft's; the controls underneath it are ordinary endpoint hardening.
items.action: Filter Recommendations > Devices > Misconfigurations by the AI-Readiness tag and read the exposed-critical-devices count first, not the score. Where Windows LAPS is not deployed on that set, that is the one to schedule.

It adds that the alerts and incidents API at /security/alerts_v2 'is not a direct, one-to-one replacement': alerts from sources that are not integrated with Microsoft 365 Defender, 'such as a Microsoft Sentinel workspace that isn't connected to the Microsoft Defender portal, or standalone and tuned alerts', are not returned by the new API. The Graph what's-new page carries the line 'Updated the retirement date for the legacy Microsoft Graph security alerts API from August 31, 2026 to October 15, 2026', read on 7 October 2026. The public source of the article, synchronised on 8 October 2026 (commit 5a88c6f), adds a fifth gap: 'Intune-originated alerts aren't available through alerts_v2. Retrieve the relevant data through the Microsoft Graph Intune APIs', and for the low-signal Exchange Online events it now names Microsoft Purview Audit and Exchange Online Message Trace as the places to read them.
items.officialTitle: Migrate from legacy alerts to the alerts and incidents API
items.fingerprintBefore: Microsoft's migration article states: 'The legacy Microsoft Graph security alerts API available through the /security/alerts endpoint is deprecated and will be retired on October 15, 2026', and 'After October 15, 2026, the legacy /security/alerts endpoint will stop returning data.' It adds that the alerts and incidents API at /security/alerts_v2 'is not a direct, one-to-one replacement': alerts from sources that are not integrated with Microsoft 365 Defender, 'such as a Microsoft Sentinel workspace that isn't connected to the Microsoft Defender portal, or standalone and tuned alerts', are not returned by the new API. The Graph what's-new page carries the line 'Updated the retirement date for the legacy Microsoft Graph security alerts API from August 31, 2026 to October 15, 2026', read on 7 October 2026.

items.fingerprint: From early 2027 the preselected enrollment type when creating an iOS or iPadOS enrollment profile changes from Device enrollment with Company Portal to Web based device enrollment, and new tenants with no enrollment profile get the web flow by default. Existing profiles are not changed. Web enrollment requires the single sign-on extension policy so that just-in-time registration can run; without it and Microsoft Authenticator, users may be unable to complete device registration. Requires iOS/iPadOS 15 or later.
items.why: Just-in-time registration is what creates the Entra device record. If the SSO extension policy is not deployed when the default flips, devices enrol into Intune but never register in Entra, so device-based Conditional Access and compliance gates have nothing to evaluate and users are blocked from protected resources.
items.action: Deploy the SSO extension policy to iOS and iPadOS now, verify Microsoft Authenticator is available on those devices, and confirm the enrollment type on every existing iOS profile at Devices > Enrollment > Apple > Enrollment Options > Enrollment types so the flip changes nothing you did not choose.

items.title: Sentinel data lake stops being a separate onboarding: one onboarding, lake tier switched on per table

items.fingerprint: Microsoft states that customers onboarding after 23 September 2026 no longer go through a separate data lake onboarding and billing setup. You onboard Microsoft Sentinel, confirm the workspace is connected to the Defender portal, then enable the lake tier per table from Table management > Retention. Total retention for existing customers evolves from archive-based retention to data lake retention after Sentinel onboarding. Interactive KQL against the lake now runs in Advanced Hunting under Investigation & Response, and the lake tier can be mirrored into Microsoft Fabric OneLake at no extra charge for federation and custom analytics. Customers who onboarded the data lake before 23 September 2026 may keep the existing documentation.
items.why: Two things a SOC has to notice. Retention changes shape: archive-based retention becomes data lake retention once the workspace is onboarded, which is a different query path and a different cost line for the same historical data. And long-term data becomes directly huntable — interactive KQL over the lake in Advanced Hunting removes the restore step that used to stand between an analyst and data older than the analytics tier.
items.action: Establish which side of 23 September the tenant onboarded on, because that decides which documentation governs it. Then, before the next retention review, check per table whether the data a hunt actually reaches for sits in the analytics tier or the lake tier, and re-time any scheduled query that assumed a restore.
