add: title: Configure Microsoft Entra Kerberos trust
description: Learn how to configure and manage Microsoft Entra Kerberos trust between Microsoft Entra ID and Active Directory Domain Services.
# Customer intent: As an IT admin, I want to configure Microsoft Entra Kerberos trust so that users can access resources by using modern credentials.

Microsoft Entra Kerberos trust establishes an inbound trust relationship in which on-premises Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) trusts Microsoft Entra ID as a Kerberos Key Distribution Center (KDC). This trust enables hybrid identity organizations to use modern credentials for applications and allows Microsoft Entra ID to become the trusted source for cloud and on-premises authentication.
This article explains how to create the Trusted Domain Object, configure clients to retrieve Kerberos tickets, rotate the Kerberos key, and remove the trust configuration.
To complete the steps in this article, you need:
- A supported Windows client that's joined to Active Directory. The domain must have a functional level of Windows Server 2012 or later.
- An on-premises Active Directory administrator account that's either a member of the Domain Admins group for the domain or a member of the Enterprise Admins group for the forest.
- A Microsoft Entra Global Administrator account.
- Hybrid identities synchronized between on-premises AD DS and Microsoft Entra ID.
## Create and configure the Microsoft Entra Kerberos Trusted Domain Object

To create and configure the Microsoft Entra Kerberos Trusted Domain Object, use the [Azure AD Hybrid Authentication Management](https://www.powershellgallery.com/packages/AzureADHybridAuthenticationManagement/) PowerShell module.
### Register the Trusted Domain Object with Microsoft Entra ID

Use the Azure AD Hybrid Authentication Management PowerShell module to set up a Trusted Domain Object in the Active Directory domain and register trust information with Microsoft Entra ID. This action creates an inbound trust relationship, which enables on-premises Active Directory to trust Microsoft Entra ID.

You only need to set up the Trusted Domain Object once per domain. If you already set up this object for your domain, skip this section and proceed to [Configure clients to retrieve Kerberos tickets](#configure-clients-to-retrieve-kerberos-tickets).
#### Install the Azure AD Hybrid Authentication Management PowerShell module
1. Start a Windows PowerShell session by using the **Run as administrator** option.
1. Install the Azure AD Hybrid Authentication Management PowerShell module by using the following script. The script:
1. Registers the PSGallery repository if it isn't already registered.
1. Configures PSGallery as a trusted repository.
1. Installs the Azure AD Hybrid Authentication Management PowerShell module.

The Azure AD Hybrid Authentication Management PowerShell module uses the AzureADPreview module, which provides advanced Microsoft Entra management features. To prevent unnecessary installation conflicts with the Azure AD PowerShell module, the installation command includes the `-AllowClobber` parameter.

roles.name: Entra SOC Identity Responder
roles.privilegedNote: Microsoft's own PRIVILEGED label now appears in the role header and on two of its four actions.
roles.description: Least-privilege identity containment from the Defender portal. Microsoft states it cannot act on privileged accounts.
roles.impact: The role this catalog has carried since 25 August as live-but-undocumented is now published. Microsoft's four actions are disable a user, enable a user, invalidate all refresh tokens and update a password — enough to take over a non-privileged account, which is why two of them carry the PRIVILEGED label. The role header carries the privileged label too, so it is in scope for PIM and for privileged-role access reviews.
roles.action: Re-run any privileged-role inventory that filtered on the published reference: this role was invisible to it until yesterday. Route assignments through PIM, add it to privileged access reviews, and alert on assignment changes.

roles.name: Security Administrator
roles.dateNote: Microsoft printed 1 September 2026 for the announcement and “the end of September 2026” for completion of rollout. The Entra role permissions reference still carries the role's pre-change action list; the newest commit touching that directory is 31 July 2026.
roles.description: Can read security information and reports, and manage configuration in Microsoft Entra ID and Office 365.
added: Disable a user account (non-privileged users) — Microsoft's wording; the role reference prints no action string yet
Enable a user account (non-privileged users) — Microsoft's wording; the role reference prints no action string yet
Revoke active sessions (non-privileged users) — Microsoft's wording; the role reference prints no action string yet
Force a password reset (non-privileged users) — Microsoft's wording; the role reference prints no action string yet
roles.impact: A role widely handed out for reading and configuring security policy becomes able to disable an account, terminate its live sessions and force a credential reset. Nobody consents to it and no assignment changes; the capability simply arrives. It is the same capability Microsoft carved into the deliberately narrow SOC Identity Responder role in June 2026.
roles.action: Pull the current holders and treat the list as a new privileged role. Move standing assignments into PIM with approval and justification, drop holders who only ever needed to read policy, and alert on Disable account, Revoke sign-in sessions and Reset user password performed by a principal holding Security Administrator.

graph.name: ThreatHunting.Read.All
graph.before: Run hunting queries — advanced hunting only, no access to stored query objects
graph.after: Run hunting queries and read saved hunting queries — plus GET /security/threathunting/queries and GET /security/threathunting/queries/{id}
graph.impact: Saved hunting queries are detection logic. Any application already consented to ThreatHunting.Read.All — typically a SOAR connector or a reporting job — can now enumerate the whole saved-query library without a new consent prompt, which means the team's coverage and its blind spots are readable by anything that could already run a hunt.
graph.action: List every service principal holding ThreatHunting.Read.All and decide, per app, whether reading the saved query library is in scope. Add GET /security/threathunting/queries to the set of Graph calls worth auditing.

graph.name: User.ReadBasic.All
graph.consent: Application: admin consent required · Delegated: not required
graph.before: returns a basic set of profile properties and, per Microsoft, also app role assignments and license details — behaviour Microsoft describes as accidental
graph.after: returns the basic profile properties only. App role assignments move to User.Read.All and license details to LicenseAssignment.Read.All
graph.impact: Two effects at once. Applications that quietly relied on the extra data break with no deprecation window — Microsoft states no sunset date. And a low-consent scope (delegated User.ReadBasic.All needs no admin consent) stops exposing licence and app-assignment data, which is reconnaissance material for anyone mapping who holds which application role.
graph.action: List service principals granted User.ReadBasic.All and check which of them read app role assignments or licence data. Applications that legitimately need it must be re-consented to User.Read.All or LicenseAssignment.Read.All, both of which require admin consent — so this is a consent-review task, not a code change.

displayText.Application: Read all users' basic profiles
displayText.Delegated: Read all users' basic profiles

descriptionByType.Application: Allows the app to read a basic set of profile properties of other users in your organization without a signed-in user. Includes display name, first and last name, email address, open extensions, and photo.
descriptionByType.Delegated: Allows the app to read a basic set of profile properties of other users in your organization on behalf of the signed-in user. This includes display name, first and last name, email address and photo.

history.note: Entered the catalog with the permission inventory baseline, parsed from Microsoft’s permissions reference.

Microsoft announced on 1 September 2026 that the permission “accidentally allows the app to read app role assignments and license details of users” and that this access is being removed. The permissions reference already describes only the basic profile properties, so the documentation does not move — the service does.

Microsoft published MC1470871 on 11 September 2026, giving the change its rollout window: general availability worldwide from mid-September 2026, expected complete by late September. The post names the replacement permissions — User.Read.All for app role assignments, LicenseAssignment.Read.All for licence details — and states the reason as a security vulnerability. The catalog entry moves from an announcement with no date to a change already rolling.

graph.dateNote: 1 September 2026 is Microsoft's own publication date for the announcement. No retirement or enforcement date is stated by Microsoft.

graph.impact: Synchronization metadata is the linkage between a source object and the object a provisioning job created from it. The ReadWrite forms can delete those object connections, which makes the next provisioning cycle treat the target account as unmatched; the Read forms expose which identities are provisioned where. Whether Entra-to-Active-Directory provisioning jobs are in scope is not stated by Microsoft (inferred that they are, because they run as service principal provisioning jobs).
graph.action: Add the four application role IDs and two delegated scope IDs to the consent watch list now. Treat a grant of SynchronizationMetadata.ReadWrite.All to anything other than the provisioning tooling you run as an incident to review.

graph.before: CloudPC.Read.All did not reach these paths before 2026-09-08.
graph.after: GET /devicemanagement/virtualendpoint/managedlicenses/retrievemanagedlicenseoperation(operationRequestId={value})
graph.impact: Cloud PC read consent gained the managed-licence operation status endpoint. Microsoft marks it least privileged for this permission in both the delegated and the application scheme, so an app already consented to CloudPC.Read.All can read managed-licence operation results from today without anything being re-consented.
graph.action: No consent prompt fires and no audit event marks the moment, so the only way to see it is to diff the endpoint map. Watch app traffic to /devicemanagement/virtualendpoint/managedlicenses/ from principals that already hold this permission.

history.note: Recorded on the afternoon pass of 8 September 2026, which re-read Microsoft's endpoint map after it moved from commit e17b679 to 0c140cd. Microsoft's file marks the path least=DelegatedWork,Application for this permission, so it is counted in leastPairs.

graph.idsNote: An endpoint-reach record is an event, not a permission entry, so it carries no AppRoleId of its own; the identifiers live on the permission's own inventory entry.

graph.originNote: Microsoft added this name to its own deployment map in the weekly permissions sync committed on 28 September 2026 at 17:00 +0300, after this brief's 06:22 pass. graph.impact: Restoring a deleted Teams channel brings its message history and files back into view. A tenant-wide restore permission is a recovery capability and an undelete capability at the same time: it can return content that a retention action or a deliberate deletion had removed from reach. It is not grantable here yet.
graph.action: Nothing to grant or revoke today. Watch for the name entering the service principal; the day it does, it becomes a consentable application permission over channel restoration and belongs in the app-consent review.
graph.descriptionNote: Microsoft publishes no consent display text or description for this permission - checked on 28 September 2026 in permissions.json (932 documented names) and in permissions-descriptions.json, and it is in neither.

graph.name: Device.ProvisionForVDI
graph.before: no published definition: no display text, no description, no privilege level, no endpoint, and isHidden true in the deployment map
graph.after: a published definition carrying display text, description, requiresAdminConsent true and privilegeLevel 3, with one path set - POST /devices/provision - and isHidden false in the deployment map
graph.originNote: Microsoft published this permission's definition in permissions/new/permissions.json in the weekly sync of 28 September 2026 at 17:00 +0300, taking that file from 931 names to 932, and in the same commit flipped isHidden from true to false in provisioningInfo.json. Checked on 28 September 2026: the Learn permissions reference page does not yet carry the name, so this is documented in Microsoft's own source file and not yet on the rendered page.
graph.impact: This permission lets an onboarded VDI provider create device objects in the directory on behalf of a signed-in user, through POST /devices/provision. A device object is an identity, and something that mints identities on a user's behalf is a write path into the directory, which is why the privilege level Microsoft assigned it is 3. Until today the name was hidden, so it could not be picked in the consent flow; from today it is visible wherever the service principal carries it.
graph.action: It is still absent from this tenant's service principal, so there is nothing to grant here yet. Where any VDI provisioning integration is in flight, note that the permission is now visible and admin-consent gated, and decide in advance who may consent to it. Re-checked every run.
